newsitem.title: USA: Jumbo Mexico, Argentina globals vie for new money.
newsitem.headline: Jumbo Mexico, Argentina globals vie for new money.

text.p: Mexico and Argentina are racing to get a head start in the sovereign issuance market with two jumbo deals to soak up the fresh funds said to be awaiting investment, analysts and fund managers said.

Mexico is offering $1 billion 10-year fixed-rate note and Argentina is expected to make its new year debut with $2 billion or even $3 billion global bond of two tranches, possibly of five-year and 15-year or 20-year tenor.

"There is new money coming in," said Walter Molano, director of emerging markets research at SBC/Warburg Securities, echoing the opinion of many analysts. "The stellar performance of emerging markets last year is drawing more new resources from mutual funds and insurance companies."
Funds from crossover buying that fuelled the emerging market rally in the second half of the year but slowed in December is expected to flow again in the new year, market sources said.
"There was a temporary hesitancy towards the end of the year when fund fund managers just wanted to lock in the performance," said a sellside source. "Now they are looking for yields again."
The supply of $3 billion to $4 billion could be placed to the satisfaction of issuers in a market still awash with liquidity, he said.
But buyside managers were more circumspect.

"Customer demand is guesswork," said a hedge fund manager, noting that the U.S. market could only absorb part of the $3 billion to $4 billion supply and the rest has to be placed in Europe and Asia where demand is hard to guage.
Another fund manager agreed that block allocation being made in proprietary books or pension funds is merely anecdotal.
Market sources in New York doubted the Argentine deal would be raised to $3 billion from $2 billion, and said the longer-maturity tranche would stay at 20-year instead of shortening to 15-year.
"Two billion is already straining the market," said a money manager, "especially on the heel of the Mexican deal."
Details of the Argentine deal will be unveiled later today by the Economy Ministry.
When push comes to shove, buyside sources said Mexico has an advantage over Argentina in terms of credit quality and outlook for upgrade.
Mexico is rated BB by Standard and Poor's and Ba2 by Moody's Investors Service, while Argentina is rated B1 and BB-minus.
But Argentina has its own strength, said Ricardo Rivera, a fixed income specialist at Santander Investments.

As a frequent and nimble issuer, Argentina has a loyal following of global investors, and its dollar-denominated debt accounted for only 24 percent of the $10 billion it raised in 1996, compared to 36 percent Deutsche mark and 19 percent in Japanese yen, he said.
Ricardo projected the yield of Argentine debts to compress by 100 to 150 basis points in 1997, bringing an estimated total return of 15 percent.

But the success of sovereign global issues depends more on managers of global bond funds moving between the sovereign holdings within their portfolios than "hard core" allocations, he said. "For example, players may sell Canadian province papers to buy Mexico."
Ultimately it is the pricing that determines how successfully the issues are placed, he said.

The Mexican 10-year bond is widely expected to be priced 310 to 315 basis points (bp) over U.S. Treasuries, while the spread for Argentine five-year is seen 280 to 288 bp and 20-year about 410-420 bp.
